etymology: Greek gnōsis, “knowledge,” from ginōskō (to know); distinct from epignōsis (full or precise knowledge, often used in the NT for the recognition-knowledge of salvation).
biblical_def: Gnōsis in the New Testament is one of the chief words for knowledge—a category that carries great theological weight in apostolic teaching about what the saint knows of God, of Christ, of salvation, of himself, and of the truth. Paul ranks knowledge among the abundances he ascribes to the Corinthian church: ye are enriched by him, in all utterance, and in all knowledge (1 Cor 1:5). He lists knowledge among the gifts of the Spirit: to another faith by the same Spirit; to another the gifts of healing by the same Spirit; To another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another discerning of spirits; to another divers kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of tongues. But all these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will (1 Cor 12:9-11). The supreme value he sets upon a particular knowledge: yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ (Phil 3:8). The knowledge Paul prizes is not abstract information but the relational and saving knowledge of the Christ who has loved him and given Himself for him. Peter sets the growth-keynote of the Christian life around the same word: but grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ (2 Pet 3:18). And the great theological doxology in Romans 11 honors the immensity of God’s own knowledge: O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! (Rom 11:33). The biblical doctrine of gnōsis has therefore both an exalted and a cautionary side. Exalted: the saint is to grow in the knowledge of Christ; the church is to be enriched in all knowledge; the depth of God’s wisdom and knowledge is worthy of doxology. Cautionary: knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth (1 Cor 8:1)—knowledge alone, divorced from love, inflates the knower rather than edifying him; and the heretical movement of the second-century church that would self-designate as Gnostics (claimants of special saving knowledge inaccessible to ordinary believers) is already prefigured in Paul’s warning to Timothy against oppositions of science (gnōsis) falsely so called (1 Tim 6:20). Biblical gnōsis is therefore the relational, saving, growing knowledge of God in Christ—held with humility, married to love, anchored in the apostolic deposit, and aimed at the doxology that the depth of God’s own knowledge invites.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines KNOWLEDGE as a clear perception of fact, truth, or duty; in scripture (rendering the Greek gnōsis), the relational and saving knowledge of God in Christ that the saint is to grow in, paired with love that the knowledge may not inflate.
webster_full: KNOWLEDGE, n. — 1. A clear and certain perception of that which exists, or of truth and fact. 2. Learning; illumination of mind. 3. Acquaintance with any fact or person. 4. Cognizance; notice. 5. In scripture, the relational and saving knowledge of God in Christ; the gift of the Spirit (1 Cor 12:8); the excellency for which all else is counted loss (Phil 3:8).
GNOSIS — (Greek term) Knowledge; especially used in 1 Cor 8:1; 12:8; 13:2, 8; 14:6; 2 Cor 6:6; 8:7; 10:5; 11:6; Eph 3:19; Phil 3:8; Col 2:3; 2 Pet 1:5-6; 3:18.
scriptures: Philippians 3:8
Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord.
2 Peter 3:18
But grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. To him be glory both now and for ever. Amen.
Romans 11:33
O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!
1 Corinthians 8:1
Now as touching things offered unto idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth.
corruption_summary: Gnōsis is corrupted, on one side, by the ancient and recurring Gnostic heresy that treats saving knowledge as a special elite possession inaccessible to ordinary believers—and on the other by the knowledge-puffs-up pattern Paul warns against, in which doctrinal precision is held without the love that would edify and produces the inflated knower rather than the built-up believer.
corruption_paragraphs: The Gnostic corruption is the most historically significant counterfeit of gnōsis. Second-century movements claiming a special saving knowledge inaccessible to ordinary believers—passed through initiation, taught by esoteric teachers, divorced from the apostolic deposit—produced what the early church recognized and refuted as a fundamental departure from the gospel. Paul’s charge to Timothy is the canonical warning: O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science (gnōsis) falsely so called (1 Tim 6:20). Biblical knowledge is not esoteric: it is the apostolic deposit set forth in the Scriptures and applied by the Spirit to every regenerate saint. The recovery against every recurrence of the Gnostic pattern (in second-century forms, in medieval mystical movements, in modern esoteric Christianity) is the same: the knowledge that saves is the knowledge of Christ as set forth in the public apostolic deposit, available to every believer through the Word and the Spirit.

The opposite corruption, more visible in the contemporary church, is the knowledge-puffs-up pattern Paul warns against in 1 Corinthians 8. Doctrinal precision is held without the love that would edify; the saint becomes more careful about doctrine and less charitable in his dealings; the very knowledge that should produce humility (the more I know of Christ, the more I see what I am) produces instead an inflated sense of one’s spiritual achievement. Paul’s remedy is precise: knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth. The cure is not less knowledge but more love—the love that, married to the knowledge, builds up both the knower and his brothers. Recover both ends. Refuse the Gnostic substitution of esoteric special knowledge for the apostolic public deposit, and refuse the knowledge-without-love pattern that inflates the knower. The biblical gnōsis is the relational, saving, growing knowledge of God in Christ, held with humility, married to love, anchored in the apostolic Word—and the church saturated with such knowledge is the church both well-instructed and visibly humble in the depth of what she has come to know.
roots_summary: Greek gnōsis (knowledge) from ginōskō (to know); cousin term epignōsis (full or precise knowledge); set against the Gnostic counterfeit (esoteric special knowledge) and the knowledge-puffs-up pattern (precision without love).
roots_lines: Greek gnōsis (G1108) — knowledge (1 Cor 1:5; 8:1; 12:8; 13:2, 8; 14:6; 2 Cor 6:6; 11:6; Eph 3:19; Phil 3:8; Col 2:3; 1 Pet 3:7; 2 Pet 1:5-6; 3:18).
Greek ginōskō (G1097) — to know, perceive, understand (the verb).
Greek epignōsis (G1922) — full or precise knowledge, recognition (Eph 1:17; 4:13; Phil 1:9; Col 1:9-10; 1 Tim 2:4; 2 Tim 2:25; Heb 10:26; 2 Pet 1:2-3, 8; 2:20).
Hebrew da‘ath (H1847) — knowledge (Prov 1:7; 2:6; Isa 11:9; Hos 4:6).
usage: The excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord—Paul counts all things loss for this relational saving knowledge.
Grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ—Peter sets the Christian life’s growth around the same word.

Gnostic counterfeit makes saving knowledge esoteric; knowledge-puffs-up pattern divorces precision from love; biblical gnōsis is the apostolic public knowledge of Christ held with humility and married to love.

etymology: Greek splagchnon, literally the inward parts, viscera, bowels; metaphorically the seat of the deepest emotions, especially compassion and tender love. Cognate verb splagchnizomai (to be moved with compassion, “moved in the bowels”).
biblical_def: Splagchnon is the Greek word literally meaning the inward parts, bowels, viscera, and metaphorically the seat of the deepest emotions—especially the seat of compassion, tender affection, and merciful sympathy. The New Testament uses the word repeatedly in this metaphorical sense, and the resulting category ‘bowels of compassion’ or ‘bowels of mercy’ is one of the most affecting in the apostolic vocabulary. The verb form splagchnizomai—literally to be moved in the bowels—is used uniformly of Christ’s compassion in the Gospels: but when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd (Matt 9:36); and Jesus, moved with compassion, put forth his hand, and touched him, and saith unto him, I will; be thou clean (Mark 1:41); and when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her, and said unto her, Weep not (Luke 7:13); but a certain Samaritan, as he journeyed, came where he was: and when he saw him, he had compassion on him (Luke 10:33); but when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him (Luke 15:20). The noun appears as the seat of the apostle’s affection: God is my record, how greatly I long after you all in the bowels of Jesus Christ (Phil 1:8); therefore receive him, that is, mine own bowels (Philem 12); and as a category the church is to put on: put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering (Col 3:12); be ye all of one mind, having compassion one of another, love as brethren, be pitiful, be courteous (1 Pet 3:8). The category therefore captures the deepest physical-emotional response to the troubles of others—the ‘gut-deep’ reaction of compassion that the Hebrew rachamim (bowels-of-mercy) located in the same body region and the Greek splagchnon retains. Biblical compassion is not chiefly sentiment but physical-emotional response; not pity-from-a-distance but the gut-felt moving toward the troubled that the verb splagchnizomai consistently names in Christ’s ministry and the apostles command for the saints.
webster_summary: (Greek term.) Splagchnon: the inward parts, viscera, bowels; metaphorically, the seat of the deepest emotions, especially compassion and tender love; in NT usage, the ‘bowels of compassion’ or ‘bowels of mercy’ on Christ’s lips and in the apostolic vocabulary.
webster_full: SPLAGCHNON — (Greek noun.) The inward parts, viscera, bowels; in NT metaphorical use, the seat of the deepest emotions, especially compassion and merciful sympathy. Bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering (Col 3:12).
COMPASSION, n. — A suffering with another; painful sympathy; pity; commiseration; that sensibility of heart which is excited by the distresses of another.
scriptures: Matthew 9:36
But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd.
Luke 10:33
But a certain Samaritan, as he journeyed, came where he was: and when he saw him, he had compassion on him.
Luke 15:20
And he arose, and came to his father. But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.
Colossians 3:12
Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering.
corruption_summary: Splagchnon-shaped compassion is corrupted, on one side, by the modernizing translations that have replaced the visceral ‘bowels of compassion’ with the colder ‘heartfelt compassion’ (losing the gut-level register the Greek physically locates)—and on the other by the sentimentalized pity-from-a-distance of contemporary feeling-but-not-moving compassion, against the Gospels’ uniform pattern of Christ moved with compassion and acting.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern translations have, with reasonable cause but real loss, replaced the KJV’s visceral bowels of mercies (Col 3:12) and bowels of Jesus Christ (Phil 1:8) with the more sanitary heart of compassion and affection of Christ Jesus. The trade is real. Bowels in modern English has acquired primarily a digestive reference that splagchnon in Greek did not carry; for the modern reader, the literal rendering produces unintended associations. But the Greek located the deepest compassions in the same body region that the Hebrew rachamim located them, and the metaphor is not random: the deepest compassions are felt in the gut, the visceral region, the body-area where the most intense emotional responses register physiologically. The KJV’s retention of the body-located metaphor preserves a sensory dimension that the modernizations lose, and the saint who reads bowels of mercies in the older idiom (with the proper understanding) recovers the visceral register the Greek word physically named.

The opposite corruption—and the more pastorally damaging one—is the sentimentalized pity-from-a-distance that has substituted feeling-but-not-moving compassion for the Gospels’ uniform pattern of Christ moved with compassion and acting. Every occurrence of splagchnizomai in the Gospels is paired with an action: He healed them; He put forth His hand; He touched the leper; He fed the multitude; He raised the widow’s son; the Samaritan went to him, bound up his wounds, brought him to the inn, paid for his care. The compassion was visceral and the action was concrete. The contemporary substitute—the awareness of suffering, the feeling of pity, the social-media expression of concern, all without the costly action that the biblical compassion uniformly produced—is not what the Gospels mean by compassion. Recover both ends. Refuse the sanitizing modernizations that lose the visceral register, and refuse the sentimentalized substitution that loses the action. Biblical splagchnon-compassion is gut-deep and act-producing—and the church saturated with such compassion is the church doing the works Christ did precisely because she has been moved as He was moved.
roots_summary: Greek splagchnon (the inward parts, bowels, viscera; metaphorically the seat of compassion) and splagchnizomai (to be moved with compassion, “moved in the bowels”)—the visceral, gut-deep compassion uniformly attributed to Christ in the Gospels and commanded of the saints in the Epistles.
roots_lines: Greek splagchnon (G4698) — the inward parts, bowels; metaphorically, seat of compassion (Luke 1:78; 2 Cor 6:12; 7:15; Phil 1:8; 2:1; Col 3:12; Philem 7, 12, 20; 1 John 3:17).
Greek splagchnizomai (G4697) — to be moved with compassion (12 NT uses, almost all of Christ; also of the Samaritan and the prodigal’s father).
Greek eusplagchnos (G2155) — good-of-the-inward-parts, tender-hearted (Eph 4:32; 1 Pet 3:8).
Hebrew rachamim (H7356) — tender mercies, compassions (the OT cousin, located in the same body region).
usage: He was moved with compassion—every occurrence of splagchnizomai in the Gospels is paired with an action; biblical compassion is gut-deep and act-producing.
Bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering—Col 3:12’s body-located vocabulary names the visceral register modern translations sanitize.

Sanitizing modernizations lose the body register; sentimentalized pity-from-a-distance loses the action; biblical splagchnon-compassion is the visceral, gut-deep, action-producing response of Christ and His saints.

etymology: Greek makrothumia, literally long-tempered-ness, from makros (long) + thumos (passion, temper). The fundamental sense is the long-restrained holding-back of righteous anger, which becomes by extension patience, longsuffering, endurance with persons.
biblical_def: Makrothumia is one of the great virtue-nouns of the New Testament, and the KJV renders it consistently as longsuffering—a coined English compound that captures the Greek’s sense better than the colorless modern patience. The word is built from makros (long) and thumos (passion, temper); its literal sense is long-tempered, the long-restrained holding-back of righteous anger that gives space and time for the offender to repent and be restored. The supreme exemplar is God Himself. He is named longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth, keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin (Ex 34:6-7—the LXX uses makrothumos); Paul says the riches of God’s longsuffering and goodness leadeth thee to repentance (Rom 2:4); Peter explains the apparent delay of Christ’s return as the Lord is not slack concerning his promise... but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance (2 Pet 3:9). God’s longsuffering is the deliberate withholding of deserved judgment to make space for repentance; the patience-shaped mercy by which the wrath is restrained while the gospel is offered. The same virtue is to characterize the saints. Makrothumia is the fourth fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22 (love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance). It is commanded as a mark of Christian community: with all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love (Eph 4:2); put on therefore... bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering (Col 3:12). It is required of ministers especially: preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine (2 Tim 4:2). The category is therefore the patient bearing-with-persons (as distinct from hupomonē, the patient bearing-with-circumstances): the deliberate, willed, sustained patience with the brother who is slow to grow, the spouse who is slow to change, the child who is slow to mature, the unbeliever who is slow to repent, the saint who has wronged us and not yet seen it. The KJV’s longsuffering is therefore a brilliant rendering: it captures the temporal-extension (long) and the suffering-with-persons (suffering) that the Greek compound names, and produces an English term that has shaped the church’s understanding of the virtue for four centuries.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines LONGSUFFERING as bearing injuries or provocations for a long time; patient; not easily provoked; in scripture, the Spirit-wrought patience with persons that is the fruit of the Spirit, modeled supremely on God’s own longsuffering toward sinners.
webster_full: LONGSUFFERING, a. — Bearing injuries or provocations for a long time; patient; not easily provoked. The Lord is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish (2 Pet 3:9).
MAKROTHUMIA — (Greek term.) Long-tempered-ness; the long-restrained holding-back of righteous anger; patience with persons; longsuffering. Listed as the fourth fruit of the Spirit in Gal 5:22.
scriptures: Galatians 5:22
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith...
Romans 2:4
Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?
2 Peter 3:9
The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance.
Colossians 3:12
Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering.
corruption_summary: Makrothumia is corrupted, on one side, by the impatience register of late-modern culture that has trained the believer to react quickly, sever relationships at the first friction, and lose the long-temper that is the Spirit-wrought patience with persons—and on the other by the despairing-presumption that mistakes God’s longsuffering for indifference and proceeds in sin as though no day of judgment will come.
corruption_paragraphs: The impatience register of late-modern culture has trained the believer out of makrothumia. The cultural patterns are uniform: immediate gratification, rapid response, severance of relationships at the first significant friction, intolerance of slow growth in others, refusal to extend the long patience with persons that the gospel commands. The believer who absorbs these patterns brings them to the church and the family: brothers are cut off for offenses that longsuffering would have absorbed, marriages are abandoned where longsuffering would have borne with the slow growth of a beloved spouse, parents grow impatient with the slow maturing of children, churches fragment over personality frictions that longsuffering would have softened. The recovery is the Spirit’s work, not human grit: makrothumia is the fruit of the Spirit, given as the Spirit fills and sanctifies the saint over time. The discipline is to ask for it, cultivate it through deliberate practice (especially with the persons whose presence most provokes its opposite), and to repent of every reactive impatience that has substituted for the long-tempered patience God Himself models.

The opposite corruption is the despairing-presumption that mistakes God’s longsuffering for indifference. Peter explicitly addresses it: the Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance. The very delay of Christ’s return that the scoffers cite as evidence God will not judge is in fact evidence of His longsuffering, deliberately extending the day of grace to give space for repentance. The presumption of those who therefore presume their sin will be tolerated forever, that the day of judgment has been canceled, that God’s patience proves His indifference, is precisely the misreading Peter refutes. Recover both ends. Refuse the impatience that has lost makrothumia as a saint’s virtue, and refuse the presumption that misreads God’s makrothumia as indifference. The biblical pattern is the saint who has received God’s longsuffering with thanksgiving, extends the same to others as the fruit the Spirit produces, and lives in sober expectation of the day when the longsuffering interval will close and the just Judge will come.
roots_summary: Greek makrothumia (long-tempered-ness, longsuffering, patience with persons), from makros (long) + thumos (passion, temper); the Spirit-wrought patience with persons (distinct from hupomonē, patience with circumstances), modeled supremely on God’s own longsuffering toward sinners.
roots_lines: Greek makrothumia (G3115) — longsuffering, patience with persons (Gal 5:22; Eph 4:2; Col 1:11; 3:12; 1 Tim 1:16; 2 Tim 3:10; 4:2; Heb 6:12; Jas 5:10; 1 Pet 3:20; 2 Pet 3:9, 15).
Greek makrothumeō (G3114) — to be longsuffering (Matt 18:26, 29; Luke 18:7; 1 Cor 13:4; 1 Thess 5:14; Heb 6:15; Jas 5:7-8; 2 Pet 3:9).
Greek makrothumos (G3116) — longsuffering (the adjective; LXX of Ex 34:6 of God).
Greek hupomonē (G5281) — patience with circumstances, endurance (the cousin virtue).
usage: The Lord is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish—God’s longsuffering deliberately extends the day of grace.
Makrothumia is the patience with persons, distinct from hupomonē, the patience with circumstances; the saint needs both.

Impatience culture loses the virtue; despairing-presumption misreads God’s longsuffering as indifference; biblical pattern is Spirit-wrought patience with persons modeled on God’s own longsuffering toward sinners.

etymology: Greek tapeinophrosunē, “lowliness of mind,” from tapeinos (low, lowly) + phronē (mind, way of thinking). The composite literally means “low-mindedness” in the inverted-from-modern-usage sense of thinking-of-oneself-as-low.
biblical_def: Tapeinophrosunē is the New Testament’s precise word for humility of mind—the inward disposition that thinks of oneself accurately (which in fallen creatures saved by grace means: low) before God and esteems others better than self before men. The word is composite: tapeinos means low, lowly, and phronē means mind or way of thinking; together they name a low-mindedness that, in modern English, has acquired the opposite sense of mean or petty—but in Greek and in apostolic usage carries the entirely positive sense of thinking-of-oneself-as-low. The word is structural to several apostolic passages. Philippians 2:3: let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves—tapeinophrosunē as the explicit antidote to strife and vainglory. The verse leads into the Christological hymn of vv. 6-8 where Christ Himself models the disposition: who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men: And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Ephesians 4:2: with all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love—tapeinophrosunē as the first of the four virtues by which the unity of the Spirit is kept in the bond of peace. Acts 20:19: Paul describes his own ministry as serving the Lord with all humility of mind, and with many tears, and temptations. Colossians 3:12: put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering. 1 Peter 5:5: likewise, ye younger, submit yourselves unto the elder. Yea, all of you be subject one to another, and be clothed with humility—the verb egkomboōmai means to tie on like an apron, picturing humility as the garment the saint puts on visibly in his dealings with others. The category is therefore precise. It is inward (a way of thinking, phronē): the actual estimate one holds of oneself before God. It is low (tapeinos): the regenerate soul, knowing both its sin and the grace by which it was saved, thinks of itself in low terms. It is consistent (a settled disposition, not occasional acts): the inward state that produces the outward life. And it is supremely Christ-shaped: the One who took the form of a servant, humbled Himself, and was obedient unto death is the model, and the conformity to His image is the long arc of the saint’s sanctification.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines HUMILITY (the closest English equivalent of tapeinophrosunē) as freedom from pride and arrogance; humbleness of mind; modest estimate of one’s own worth; in scripture, the inward Spirit-wrought disposition modeled supremely on Christ’s own self-humbling.
webster_full: HUMILITY, n. — In ethics, freedom from pride and arrogance; humbleness of mind; a modest estimate of one’s own worth. In theology, that lowness of mind which is the disposition of the saint redeemed by grace, having a just sense of his sin and of God’s mercy in Christ. In lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves (Phil 2:3).

TAPEINOPHROSUNE — (Greek term.) Lowliness of mind; humility; the inward Spirit-wrought disposition of thinking-of-oneself-as-low. Found at Phil 2:3; Eph 4:2; Acts 20:19; Col 2:18, 23 (in counterfeit form); 3:12; 1 Pet 5:5.
scriptures: Philippians 2:3
Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.
Ephesians 4:2
With all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love.
Colossians 3:12
Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering.
1 Peter 5:5
Likewise, ye younger, submit yourselves unto the elder. Yea, all of you be subject one to another, and be clothed with humility: for God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble.
corruption_summary: Tapeinophrosunē is corrupted, on one side, by the assertiveness-culture of the present age that has redefined humility as weakness and trained the believer to despise the very disposition Christ Himself models—and on the other by the false humility Paul explicitly warns against in Col 2:18, 23 (the performed self-deprecation that retains the inward pride while displaying the outward token).
corruption_paragraphs: The assertiveness-culture corruption is the most pervasive contemporary one. The cultural script is clear: lean in, know your worth, assert yourself, refuse to be made small, take up space. The Spirit-shaped disposition Paul commands—in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves—sounds to such ears like an invitation to weakness and oppression. But the inversion is the inner shape of the kingdom, modeled by the King who, being in the form of God, took upon Himself the form of a servant. The cure is the Christological pattern: the Christ-shaped soul learns that the way up in the kingdom is down, that the great are the servants, that he who humbles himself shall be exalted. Recover the doctrine, and the saint recovers also the freedom and dignity of the lower seat—the freedom from the exhausting labor of self-promotion and the dignity of walking the road his Master walked.

The opposite corruption is the false humility (literally, in Col 2:18, ethelothrēskia — will-worship paired with tapeinophrosunē) that Paul explicitly warns against: the performed self-deprecation that retains the inward pride while displaying the outward token. The performed humility takes various forms: the carefully curated self-deprecation that announces its own modesty; the boast disguised as confession (my biggest weakness is that I work too hard); the ascetic display that uses external rigor to flatter the soul; the visible token of low estimation offered for social credit. Paul names it precisely because it counterfeits the real virtue. The cure is the inward work: confess what is actually true, take the lower seat in reality, esteem others better in fact, refuse the inward boast that the performance was meant to mask. Recover both ends. Refuse the assertiveness-culture that despises the very disposition Christ models, and refuse the performed false humility that retains the inward pride. The biblical tapeinophrosunē is the inward thing, all the way through—the actual estimate of oneself before God, settled into the consistent disposition that produces both the words and the life of one conformed in measure to the lowly Christ.
roots_summary: Greek tapeinophrosunē from tapeinos (low) + phronē (mind, way of thinking): the inward Spirit-wrought disposition of thinking-of-oneself-as-low, modeled supremely on Christ’s own self-humbling (Phil 2:3-8), structural to apostolic ethics.
roots_lines: Greek tapeinophrosunē (G5012) — lowliness of mind, humility (Acts 20:19; Eph 4:2; Phil 2:3; Col 2:18, 23; 3:12; 1 Pet 5:5).
Greek tapeinos (G5011) — low, lowly, humble (the adjective; used of Christ’s heart in Matt 11:29).
Greek tapeinoō (G5013) — to make low, humble (James 4:10; 1 Pet 5:6; Phil 2:8 of Christ’s self-humbling).
Greek phronē (G5424) — understanding, mind (the second element of the compound).
usage: In lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves—Paul’s explicit command leading directly into the Christological hymn of Phil 2:6-11.
Tapeinophrosunē is the inward state (a way of thinking, phronē) that produces the outward life; the actual estimate of oneself before God, not the performance for human view.

Assertiveness-culture redefines humility as weakness; false humility performs the token while retaining the inward pride; biblical tapeinophrosunē is the Christ-shaped inward disposition, all the way through.

etymology: Greek paraklēsis, “a calling-alongside,” from parakaleō (to call alongside), from para- (alongside) + kaleō (to call). The semantic range covers exhortation, encouragement, consolation, and (in the noun form paraklētos) advocate, comforter, the Holy Spirit.
biblical_def: Paraklēsis is one of the most semantically rich words in the New Testament. The verb parakaleō means literally to call alongside, and the noun paraklēsis names the action of calling-alongside in its several biblical applications: exhortation, encouragement, consolation, comfort. The same root produces paraklētos, the title Christ applies to the Holy Spirit in John 14–16: the Comforter, the Advocate, the One called alongside the believer to teach, witness, convict, comfort, and abide forever. The semantic range is therefore wide, and the same Greek word can do work that English needs three or four words to do. In exhortation: he that exhorteth, on exhortation (Rom 12:8); but exhort one another daily, while it is called To day (Heb 3:13—the verb behind exhort). In encouragement: now the God of patience and consolation grant you to be likeminded one toward another (Rom 15:5); that ye might be comforted together with you by the mutual faith both of you and me (Rom 1:12—paraklēthēnai). In consolation: blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort; Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God (2 Cor 1:3-4—the noun paraklēsis and the verb together five times in the verse). In Christ’s naming of the Spirit: and I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever (John 14:16—paraklētos). The biblical pattern is therefore that paraklēsis is the rich Spirit-mediated ministry by which the gospel-truth is brought to bear upon the soul in the precise mode that soul most needs in the moment: as exhortation for the drifting saint, as encouragement for the discouraged, as consolation for the bereaved, as advocacy for the accused. The Spirit Himself is the paraklētos, and the ministry the apostles, the elders, and the saints perform is derivative of His: they call alongside one another with the gospel-truth as the Spirit teaches, applies, and brings home. The category is structural to apostolic ministry. Paul’s epistles are saturated with the verb and noun; his pastoral approach is parakletic (calling-alongside) before it is anything else; the church is to be a community in which the ministry of paraklēsis is mutually exercised by every Spirit-filled saint.
webster_summary: (Greek term.) Paraklēsis: a calling-alongside; the rich Spirit-mediated ministry by which the gospel-truth is brought to bear upon the soul as exhortation, encouragement, consolation, or advocacy according to the need of the hour. The Holy Spirit is the paraklētos par excellence; saints exercise derivative paraklēsis in the body.
webster_full: PARAKLESIS — (Greek noun, G3874.) A calling-alongside; exhortation; encouragement; consolation; comfort. The cognate paraklētos (G3875) is Christ’s title for the Holy Spirit (John 14:16, 26; 15:26; 16:7) and is applied to Christ Himself in 1 John 2:1 (we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous).

COMFORTER, n. — One who administers comfort or consolation; one who strengthens and supports under affliction or calamity. The Holy Spirit is so called by Christ. I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter (John 14:16).
scriptures: 2 Corinthians 1:3-4

Blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort; Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God.
John 14:16
And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever.
Romans 12:8
Or he that exhorteth, on exhortation: he that giveth, let him do it with simplicity; he that ruleth, with diligence; he that sheweth mercy, with cheerfulness.
Hebrews 3:13
But exhort one another daily, while it is called To day; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.
corruption_summary: Paraklēsis is corrupted, in the contemporary church, by the splitting of its rich semantic unity into separated specialties (the exhorter does not console, the consoler does not exhort, the encourager does not call-alongside in any substantive sense)—and by the loss of the Spirit-mediated character of the ministry, treating paraklēsis as a human pastoral skill rather than as the Spirit’s own work through Spirit-filled saints.
corruption_paragraphs: The semantic richness of paraklēsis has been split in the contemporary church into separated specialties whose practitioners often do not overlap. The exhorter (the strong preacher who confronts) is a different person from the consoler (the grief-counselor); the encourager (the affirming friend) is a different person from the advocate (the lawyer or pastoral defender). The Greek word and the biblical pattern hold these together: paraklēsis is the rich Spirit-mediated ministry by which the gospel-truth is brought to bear upon the soul in the mode that soul most needs in the moment—exhortation, encouragement, consolation, advocacy—by the same Spirit working through the same called-alongside saint. The recovery is the recovery of integrated parakletic ministry: saints who can call alongside one another with whatever the moment requires, whether that is the hard word of exhortation or the tender word of consolation, and elders who can do the whole work of the gospel ministry rather than only its narrow specialties.

The deeper corruption is the loss of the Spirit-mediated character of the ministry. Christ’s explicit teaching is that the paraklētos par excellence is the Holy Spirit, and that the parakletic ministry the apostles and saints perform is derivative of His. The Spirit calls alongside through them; the truth they bring is applied to the soul by Him; the comfort consoled with is the comfort wherewith they themselves were comforted of God (2 Cor 1:4). Where this Spirit-mediated character is lost, paraklēsis becomes a human pastoral skill—techniques of counseling, practices of encouragement, methods of exhortation—divorced from the dependence on the Spirit’s working that the apostolic pattern requires. Recover both ends. Restore the semantic integration of the rich biblical ministry, and restore the Spirit-mediated character of the ministry. The saint who calls alongside another saint with the gospel-truth, in dependence on the Spirit who is Himself the great Paraklētos, is exercising the very ministry the apostles named—and the church saturated with such mutual parakletic ministry is the church in which the Comforter’s own work is mediated through the body of Christ to every member who is in need.

The Holy Spirit is the paraklētos par excellence; saints exercise derivative parakletic ministry; the church saturated with such ministry mediates the Comforter’s own work to its members.

etymology: Greek plērophoria, “full assurance, full conviction,” from plēro- (full) + phor- (to bear). The literal sense is “full-bearing” or “full-carrying”: the soul borne fully into conviction.
biblical_def: Plērophoria is the New Testament’s rich word for full assurance—the settled, undoubting, soul-borne conviction of the truth of the gospel, the love of God in Christ, the hope of glory, and the believer’s own standing in the salvation announced. The word is rare in the New Testament (four uses) but each is theologically weighty. Colossians 2:2: Paul labors for the saints that their hearts might be comforted, being knit together in love, and unto all riches of the full assurance of understanding, to the acknowledgement of the mystery of God, and of the Father, and of Christ. Hebrews 6:11: and we desire that every one of you do shew the same diligence to the full assurance of hope unto the end. Hebrews 10:22: let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water. 1 Thessalonians 1:5: for our gospel came not unto you in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Ghost, and in much assurance. The four uses cluster into a structural doctrine. The saints are to have full assurance of understanding: the settled comprehension of God’s mystery in Christ. They are to have full assurance of hope: the settled expectation of the inheritance reserved in heaven. They are to have full assurance of faith: the settled confidence of access to the throne of grace by the blood of Jesus. And the gospel itself comes with much assurance when the Spirit accompanies the Word. Plērophoria is therefore not presumption—not the soul claiming what God has not given—but the Spirit-wrought settled persuasion of what God has in fact given: the full conviction of mind, heart, and will, that what the gospel announces is true and that the believer is included in it. The doctrine is pastorally crucial. Where assurance is absent, the saint is restless, fearful, unable to draw near with full confidence; where assurance is present, the saint can stand at the throne, walk in his calling, suffer in his trial, and die in his Lord with the settled inward certainty that what has been announced is true and that he is in it. The Reformed tradition has emphasized that plērophoria is the privilege of every believer (against traditions that have made assurance a privileged second blessing reserved for the few), is grounded in the objective work of Christ rather than the believer’s introspection (against the despair of self-examination divorced from the gospel), and is ordinarily produced by the Spirit’s witness to the Word that announces Christ. The recovery of plērophoria is therefore the recovery of the saint’s rest in what God has done.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines FULL ASSURANCE (a phrase rendering the Greek plērophoria) as entire, settled certainty of mind; the Spirit-wrought conviction of the truth of the gospel and of the believer’s standing in it; in scripture, the privilege of every believer through the Spirit’s witness to the Word.
webster_full: ASSURANCE, n. — The act of assuring, or making certain or sure to one’s self; certainty. In divinity, the firm persuasion of one’s reconciliation to God, and of his salvation by faith in Christ; full and certain confidence. Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith (Heb 10:22).
PLEROPHORIA — (Greek noun, G4136.) Full assurance, full conviction. Four NT uses: Col 2:2; 1 Thess 1:5; Heb 6:11; 10:22. Etymologically full-bearing: the soul borne fully into settled conviction.
scriptures: Colossians 2:2

That their hearts might be comforted, being knit together in love, and unto all riches of the full assurance of understanding, to the acknowledgement of the mystery of God, and of the Father, and of Christ.
Hebrews 6:11
And we desire that every one of you do shew the same diligence to the full assurance of hope unto the end.
Hebrews 10:22
Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water.
1 Thessalonians 1:5
For our gospel came not unto you in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Ghost, and in much assurance; as ye know what manner of men we were among you for your sake.
corruption_summary: Plērophoria is corrupted, on one side, by the presumption that claims assurance as a possession independent of any examination, divorcing it from the marks of regenerate life Scripture supplies—and on the other by the despair that withholds assurance as a privileged possession of the few, against the apostolic pattern that addresses ordinary saints with full-assurance language as the normal Christian standing.
corruption_paragraphs: Presumption is one corruption of plērophoria: the claim of assurance as a possession independent of any examination, divorced from the marks of regenerate life Scripture supplies. The believer who has prayed a sinner’s prayer at some past moment, who has placed himself in the category of Christian, and who therefore presumes upon assurance without any present marks of regenerate life—repentance, faith working through love, growth in holiness, the inward witness of the Spirit—has converted the biblical doctrine into a self-flattering presumption Scripture does not support. The Bible holds assurance and self-examination together: examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates? (2 Cor 13:5). The recovery is the holding together: the gospel-grounded assurance that the work of Christ is sufficient for sinners, paired with the careful self-examination that confirms the marks of regenerate life are present in fact.

The opposite corruption is the despair that withholds assurance from ordinary saints as if it were a privileged possession reserved for the unusually mature, the unusually pious, or those who have passed through some specific spiritual experience the rest have not. The Reformed tradition’s sustained insistence has been that plērophoria is the privilege of every believer—the normal Christian standing, addressed by the apostles to ordinary saints in their ordinary letters—and that the absence of assurance is a problem to be remedied rather than a humility to be embraced. The Westminster Confession (18.3): this infallible assurance doth not so belong to the essence of faith, but that a true believer may wait long, and conflict with many difficulties, before he be partaker of it: yet, being enabled by the Spirit to know the things which are freely given him of God, he may, without extraordinary revelation, in the right use of ordinary means, attain thereunto. Recover both ends. Refuse the presumption that claims assurance apart from the marks of regenerate life, and refuse the despair that withholds it from ordinary saints. The biblical plērophoria is the Spirit-wrought settled conviction of what God has given, grounded in the objective gospel and confirmed by the Spirit’s witness to the marks of regenerate life—the rest in the Father’s love that the apostles uniformly assume their hearers can know.
roots_summary: Greek plērophoria (full assurance, full conviction) from plēro- (full) + phor- (to bear): the soul borne fully into settled conviction. Four NT uses (Col 2:2; 1 Thess 1:5; Heb 6:11; 10:22), structurally clustering into assurance of understanding, hope, and faith; the privilege of every believer through the Spirit’s witness to the Word.

Plērophoria is the privilege of every believer through the Spirit’s witness to the Word, not a privileged possession of the few.

Presumption claims assurance apart from regenerate marks; despair withholds it from ordinary saints; biblical pattern grounds assurance in the gospel and confirms it by the Spirit’s witness to the marks of new life.

etymology: Greek kurios, “lord, master, owner,” the great LXX/NT translation of the Hebrew YHWH (the divine Name, rendered the LORD in the KJV) and Adonai (Lord); also used of Jesus Christ in the NT as His distinctive divine title.
biblical_def: Kurios is the great Greek title of lordship—the word used in the LXX to translate both the divine Name YHWH (rendered the LORD in the KJV) and the Hebrew title Adonai (Lord), and used in the New Testament as Jesus’s distinctive divine title. The Christological weight is enormous. When the New Testament writers call Jesus kurios, they are not using a polite social honorific (though the word can carry that lesser sense in some contexts); they are using the very word their Greek-reading Bibles used for God Himself. The early Christian confession Jesus is Lord (kurios Iēsous) is therefore in its first-century context a confession of His deity, His co-identity with the LORD of the Old Testament, and His authority over all creation. Paul makes the equation explicit: that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth; And that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (kurios Iēsous Christos), to the glory of God the Father (Phil 2:10-11)—quoting Isaiah 45:23, where the One before whom every knee bows is YHWH Himself, and applying it directly to Jesus Christ as kurios. Romans 10:9: that if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved. The confession of Jesus as Lord is the saving confession because it is the recognition of His deity and the submission to His authority that grace produces in the heart. The early church’s persecutors knew exactly what the confession claimed: the Roman demand that Christians say Caesar is Lord (kurios Kaisar) and the martyrs’ refusal—kurios Iēsous, not kurios Kaisar—was the political-theological flashpoint that put many of them to death. Beyond the Christological weight, kurios functions across the New Testament in its full lordship-sense. The Lord whose will is to be done; the Lord whose word is to be obeyed; the Lord whose service is the saint’s vocation; the Lord whose return is to be awaited; the Lord who will judge the living and the dead. The recovery of the title in its full biblical weight is structural to recovered Christian discipleship: Jesus is not merely Savior (a doctrine the lordship-truncated gospel of certain contemporary traditions emphasizes alone) but Lord, and the same Jesus who saved is the Lord whose authority over the saint is comprehensive.
webster_summary: (Greek term.) Kurios: lord, master, owner; the LXX/NT word for the Hebrew divine Name YHWH and for the title Adonai; Jesus’s distinctive NT divine title, the confession Jesus is Lord being the early Christian recognition of His deity and authority over all creation.
webster_full: LORD, n. — 1. A master; a person possessing supreme power and authority. 2. In the scripture, the Supreme Being; Jehovah. When LORD is in small capitals, it represents the Hebrew Jehovah. When written Lord, it represents the Hebrew Adonai. In the New Testament Lord answers to the Greek Kurios, and is applied especially to Jesus Christ as the divine title confessing His deity.
KURIOS — (Greek noun.) Lord, master, owner. The LXX translation of YHWH (rendered LORD) and Adonai (rendered Lord); in the NT, Jesus’s distinctive divine title (over 700 uses).
scriptures: Philippians 2:9-11

Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name: That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth; And that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
Romans 10:9

1 Corinthians 12:3
Wherefore I give you to understand, that no man speaking by the Spirit of God calleth Jesus accursed: and that no man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost.
Acts 2:36
Therefore let all the house of Israel know assuredly, that God hath made that same Jesus, whom ye have crucified, both Lord and Christ.
corruption_summary: Kurios is corrupted, on one side, by the lordship salvation controversy of certain contemporary traditions that have separated Savior from Lord and made Christ’s lordship optional to His saviorhood—and on the other by the casual contemporary use of Lord Jesus as a polite religious phrase shorn of the deity-confessing, authority-establishing weight the early Christian use of kurios Iēsous carried as the political-theological flashpoint of martyrdom.
corruption_paragraphs: The lordship salvation controversy of recent decades exposed a long-running corruption in certain evangelical traditions that had separated Savior from Lord: the gospel was preached as accept Jesus as Savior, with the question of His lordship over the saint’s life deferred or left optional. The biblical pattern refuses the separation. Romans 10:9 makes the confession kurios Iēsous structural to saving faith: the same Jesus who is Savior is Lord, and the confession of Him as Lord is the recognition of His deity, His authority, and the saint’s submission to Him as such. The recovery is the recovery of the integrated gospel: Christ is Savior and Lord in one indivisible person, and the saving confession received Him as such. The contemporary truncated gospel that omits His lordship has produced what its critics rightly called cheap grace: a Christianity in which Jesus is acknowledged as helpful for the afterlife while the present life is conducted as if His lordship over it had never been established.

The opposite contemporary corruption is the casual use of Lord Jesus as a polite religious phrase shorn of the deity-confessing, authority-establishing weight the early Christian use of kurios Iēsous carried. The martyrs of the early centuries went to lions and to fire for the refusal to say kurios Kaisar and the insistence on kurios Iēsous; the political-theological flashpoint of that confession was its explicit denial of Caesar’s ultimate lordship and its insistence that Jesus alone is Lord. Contemporary believers often invoke the same title without any sense of its weight: Lord Jesus as a verbal habit in prayer, the Lord as a religious code-word, Lord and Savior as a familiar phrase—but with no operative sense that the confession is the recognition of a deity, the establishment of an authority, the political-theological staking of one’s allegiance against every rival lord. Recover both ends. Refuse the lordship-omitting truncated gospel, and refuse the casual emptying of the deity-confession that kurios Iēsous in its first-century context carried. Jesus is Lord—the LORD of the Old Testament, the only Lord, the Lord whose authority over the saint’s life is comprehensive, the Lord whose return is the consummating event of history. The confession is everything, and the church saturated with the confession in its full weight is the church the apostles built and the martyrs died for.

etymology: Greek theos, “God,” the LXX/NT word for the Hebrew Elohim (God) and occasionally for El; the chief noun for the deity throughout both testaments’ Greek text.
biblical_def: Theos is the New Testament’s chief noun for God—the word used in the LXX to translate the Hebrew Elohim (the most common Hebrew word for God) and occasionally El, and used throughout the New Testament as the standard designation for the deity. The word is so structural that the New Testament’s opening verses can scarcely move without it: in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God (theos), and the Word was God (theos) (John 1:1)—a verse that has structured Christian Trinitarian thought from the second century onward and that contains within it the deepest claim the apostles make about the deity of Christ. Two of the verse’s three uses of theos are articular (with the definite article ho theos) and one is anarthrous (without the article, simply theos); both grammatically distinct uses claim full deity, the second clause naming the Word as the same theos with whom He was eternally. The New Testament uses theos in several major theological contexts. Of the Father: God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son (John 3:16); blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ (2 Cor 1:3). Of the Son: and the Word was God (John 1:1); Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God (John 20:28); that we may know him that is true, and we are in him that is true, even in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God, and eternal life (1 John 5:20); but unto the Son he saith, Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever (Heb 1:8 quoting Ps 45:6); looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ (Tit 2:13); through the righteousness of God and our Saviour Jesus Christ (2 Pet 1:1). Of the Holy Spirit: the deity of the Spirit is implied by His person and work, though the explicit titular application of theos to the Spirit is rarer than to the Father and Son; Acts 5:3-4 sets the inference: Peter says Ananias has lied to the Holy Ghost and immediately to theos, making the equation. The doctrine of God in the New Testament is therefore structured around theos in its full applications: one God (Deut 6:4; 1 Cor 8:6; Eph 4:6), eternally existing in three persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—each of whom is properly named theos, sharing the one divine essence, distinguishable by their personal properties and relations. The Trinitarian doctrine the church confesses across the creeds is built upon the New Testament’s precise applications of theos to the three persons in their unity and distinction. Apart from the doctrine of God, every other doctrine collapses; with the doctrine of God set out from the New Testament’s use of theos, the whole Christian theology stands.
webster_summary: (Greek term.) Theos: God; the LXX/NT word for the Hebrew Elohim; the chief noun designating the deity throughout the NT; applied to the Father, Son, and (by inference) the Holy Spirit in their unity and distinction as the One God in three persons.
webster_full: GOD, n. — The Supreme Being; Jehovah; the eternal and infinite Spirit, the Creator, and the Sovereign of the universe. In scripture, applied principally to the True God, but also occasionally to false gods (with qualification), to angels, and to magistrates as representatives of divine authority.
THEOS — (Greek noun, G2316.) God; the chief NT noun for the deity. Over 1300 NT uses. Applied to the Father, Son, and (by inference) the Holy Spirit; the foundation of Trinitarian doctrine.
scriptures: John 1:1
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
John 20:28
And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God.
Titus 2:13
Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ.
1 John 5:20

And we know that the Son of God is come, and hath given us an understanding, that we may know him that is true, and we are in him that is true, even in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God, and eternal life.
corruption_summary: Theos is corrupted, in the contemporary religious landscape, by the generic-deism that treats God as a neutral category occupied differently by different religions—and by the heretical anti-Trinitarian movements (Arianism in its many recurrences, modalism in its modern forms, Jehovah’s Witness denial of Christ’s deity, Unitarianism) that refuse the New Testament’s precise application of theos to the Son and (by inference) the Holy Spirit alongside the Father.
corruption_paragraphs: Generic-deism is the contemporary cultural corruption of theos. The category God is treated as a neutral, common, religiously-pluralistic noun occupied differently by Christianity, Islam, Judaism, Hinduism (in its monotheistic strands), and the deism of philosophical theists. The implication—that the various religions are all reaching for the same God under different conceptions—is not what Scripture means by theos. The God of the Bible is the specific Trinity: one in essence, three in persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. To worship the God of the Bible is to worship the Trinity; to refuse the Trinity (as Islam, Judaism since the rejection of Christ, Unitarianism, and the various Christian heresies do) is to worship a different deity, however much the vocabulary overlaps. The recovery is the precise Trinitarian doctrine. The God Christians worship is not God in the generic sense but the Father, the Son Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit, one God in three persons; the gospel announces the Father’s love for the world expressed in the Son’s incarnation, cross, and resurrection, applied by the Holy Spirit; the saint is baptized in the name (singular) of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost; the very Christian identity is constituted by the Trinity.

The heretical anti-Trinitarian movements are the historic corruption that the orthodox church has confronted across every generation. Arianism in the fourth century denied the Son’s full deity, making Him a created firstborn; Nicaea confessed instead theos ek theou, phōs ek phōtos, theos alēthinos ek theou alēthinou, gennetheis ou poiētheis, homoousios tōi patri—God of God, Light of Light, true God of true God, begotten not made, of one substance with the Father. Modalism (in its various ancient and modern forms) denies the distinct persons, treating Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as modes or manifestations of one person; the orthodox tradition has consistently confessed the three distinct persons in one essence. Modern movements—Jehovah’s Witnesses denying Christ’s deity, Unitarianism reducing the Trinity to one person, certain Word-of-Faith and Oneness Pentecostal movements distorting the Trinity in various ways—are the contemporary recurrences of the same ancient errors. The recovery is the precise New Testament application of theos: to the Father (uniformly), to the Son (explicitly in John 1:1; 20:28; Heb 1:8; Titus 2:13; 2 Pet 1:1; 1 John 5:20), and (by inference) to the Holy Spirit (Acts 5:3-4)—one God in three persons, eternally distinguished, eternally united, the Trinity Christians worship and the only true God.
roots_summary: Greek theos (God): the chief NT noun for the deity, LXX translation of the Hebrew Elohim; applied to the Father, Son, and (by inference) the Holy Spirit; the foundation of Trinitarian doctrine and the structural noun of Christian theology.

Hebrew Elohim (H430) — God (the most common Hebrew word for God; the plural form with singular verb agreement signaling the divine plurality-in-unity later articulated in Trinitarian doctrine).

My Lord and my God—Thomas’s confession after the resurrection is the disciple’s explicit recognition of Christ’s deity.
Generic-deism flattens theos into a religiously-neutral category; anti-Trinitarian heresies refuse its precise NT applications; biblical theos is the One God in three persons whom Christians worship.

etymology: Hebrew b’rīth, “covenant,” possibly from a root meaning to cut (as in karat b’rīth, “to cut a covenant”) or possibly from a root meaning to bind. The Hebrew structural keyword for the binding pact between parties, especially the binding pact between God and His people.
biblical_def: B’rīth is the great Hebrew structural noun for covenant—the binding pact, formally ratified, by which God enters into structured relationship with His people across redemptive history. The word appears about 280 times in the Old Testament, and its uses cluster into the great covenantal moments: the covenant with Noah after the flood (Gen 9:8-17), the covenant with Abraham (Gen 15, 17), the covenant at Sinai (Ex 19-24), the covenant with David (2 Sam 7), and the prophesied new covenant in Jeremiah 31:31-34 fulfilled in Christ. Each of these is a b’rīth, and each carries the structural marks of biblical covenants: a divine initiative (God comes to His people), formal stipulations (commands, promises, signs), formal ratification (often by sacrificial blood—hence karat b’rīth, “to cut a covenant,” the cutting referring to the cutting of the sacrificial victims by which the covenant was ratified), and ongoing structured relationship (the covenant community lives under the terms of its covenant). The covenant-structure is therefore the deep organizing principle of biblical theology. God does not relate to His people as the random deity of paganism, demanding propitiation now and tolerating neglect then; He relates by covenant—by formally ratified, structurally articulated, historically progressive arrangement. The history of redemption unfolds as the history of God’s covenants, each building on the one before, each pointing forward to the consummate one. The New Testament continues the structure, with diathēkē (covenant) as the Greek equivalent of b’rīth. Christ Himself at the Last Supper says: this is my blood of the new testament (diathēkē, covenant), which is shed for many for the remission of sins (Matt 26:28). Hebrews develops the doctrine at length: Christ is the mediator of a better covenant, established upon better promises, the eternal covenant whose blood is the blood of Christ. The covenant-structure is therefore not an OT-only theological curiosity but the structural reality within which the gospel itself stands: the new covenant in Christ’s blood, into which the saints are admitted by faith and baptism, under which they live with God’s law written on their hearts and the Spirit indwelling them as the seal of the covenant. The recovery of covenantal theology in any age is the recovery of the structural reality within which the gospel itself stands: a covenantal God making covenantal promises and bringing them to fulfillment in the covenantal Christ whose blood is the blood of the new covenant.
webster_summary: (Hebrew term.) B’rīth: covenant; the binding pact, formally ratified, by which God enters into structured relationship with His people across redemptive history; the structural keyword of OT theology and (as Greek diathēkē) of NT theology as well.
webster_full: COVENANT, n. — In law, a mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or to forbear some act or thing; a contract. In theology, the various special arrangements by which God brings men into relation with Himself, as the covenant of works with Adam, the covenant of grace with Abraham and his seed, and the new covenant in Christ’s blood.

corruption_summary: B’rīth-shaped covenantal theology is corrupted, on one side, by the dispensational fragmentation that has divided redemptive history into separated dispensations with weakened covenantal continuity—and on the other by the supersessionist replacement-theology that has read the new covenant as cancelling rather than fulfilling God’s prior covenant promises, especially to Israel.
corruption_paragraphs: Strict dispensational systems have, in their classical forms, fragmented redemptive history into separated dispensations (innocence, conscience, government, promise, law, grace, kingdom) with weakened covenantal continuity between them. Each dispensation has its own administration; the church and Israel are sharply distinguished as separate peoples of God with separate covenantal trajectories; the unity of God’s covenantal dealing across redemptive history is muted. The covenantal tradition (Reformed, Presbyterian, classically Reformed Baptist) has preserved instead the structural unity: one covenant of grace, administered differently in the Old and New Testaments, fulfilled in Christ, in which the people of God (Israel under the Old, the church gathered from Jew and Gentile under the New) are essentially one. The recovery of covenantal continuity is the recovery of the structural unity of the Bible: one God making one covenant of grace, progressively unfolded across redemptive history, consummated in the one mediator Jesus Christ.

The opposite corruption is the supersessionist replacement-theology that reads the new covenant as cancelling rather than fulfilling God’s prior covenant promises, especially to Israel. The new covenant is presented as displacing the old; the Jewish people are read out of God’s purposes; the Christian church is treated as the sole heir of the promises with no remaining future role for ethnic Israel. Paul refuses this in Romans 9-11. The promises to Israel have not been annulled; the Jewish rejection of Christ has not removed Israel from God’s covenantal dealings; the future ingathering of Israel is itself part of the covenantal unfolding (and so all Israel shall be saved, Rom 11:26). Recover both ends. Refuse the dispensational fragmentation that fragments God’s covenants, and refuse the supersessionist replacement that reads the new as cancelling rather than fulfilling the prior. The biblical covenantal pattern is one God, one covenant of grace, progressively administered, consummated in Christ, with Jew and Gentile gathered into the one people of God under the new covenant Christ has ratified in His blood—and the recovery of covenantal theology in this proper form is the recovery of the structural unity within which the gospel itself stands.
roots_summary: Hebrew b’rīth (covenant, the binding pact); cognate verb-phrase karat b’rīth (to cut a covenant); Greek NT equivalent diathēkē—the structural keyword of biblical theology, naming the binding, formally ratified relationship by which God brings His people into structured relationship across redemptive history.

Dispensational fragmentation weakens covenantal continuity; supersessionist replacement reads the new covenant as cancelling rather than fulfilling the prior; biblical covenantal theology is one God, one covenant of grace, progressively unfolded, consummated in Christ.

etymology: Hebrew tselem, “image, likeness, representation,” from a root meaning to carve or to shadow. The Greek LXX renders it eikōn, image; the NT picks up the language for Christ as the eikōn of the invisible God.
biblical_def: Tselem is the Hebrew word for image or likeness, and its supreme biblical occurrence is at the creation of man in Genesis 1:26-27: and God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness... So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them. The doctrine that flows from this single text is one of the deepest in biblical anthropology. Every human being is created in the image of God (tselem ’Elohim): male and female, child and adult, born and unborn, intelligent and developmentally disabled, healthy and dying, of every ethnicity and tribe—each bears the image of the Creator and is to be treated accordingly. The image-doctrine grounds the biblical sanctity of human life (Gen 9:6: whoso sheddeth man’s blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man—capital punishment for murder grounded explicitly in the image), the biblical equality of all human persons (every person bears the image, regardless of natural distinctions), and the biblical dignity of every neighbor (James 3:9 grounds the warning against cursing one’s fellow-man in the fact that therewith curse we men, which are made after the similitude of God). The fall has marred the image but has not erased it: Adam after the fall begets Seth in his own likeness, after his image (Gen 5:3)—the image persists in fallen humanity, though damaged. Christ is the perfect image: Colossians 1:15, who is the image (eikōn) of the invisible God; 2 Corinthians 4:4, the light of the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the image of God; Hebrews 1:3, the express image of his person. The redemptive trajectory of the doctrine is the restoration and consummation of the image in the redeemed. The saints are being renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him (Col 3:10); they are predestinated to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren (Rom 8:29); and at the consummation, we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). The image-doctrine therefore traces a structural arc across the canon: created in the image, marred by the fall, restored in Christ the perfect image, progressively renewed in His people through sanctification, consummated at the resurrection when the saints shall fully bear the image of the heavenly. Apart from the image-doctrine, biblical anthropology collapses; with it, the dignity of every human person, the equality of all bearers of the image, and the trajectory of the redeemed toward conformity to Christ all stand.
webster_summary: (Hebrew term.) Tselem: image, likeness, representation; the Hebrew word at the creation of man (Gen 1:26-27, in the image of God); the foundational anthropological doctrine grounding the dignity of every human person and the redemptive trajectory toward conformity to Christ, the perfect image (Col 1:15).
webster_full: IMAGE, n. — A representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance, as wood, stone, brass, or marble. In scripture, the resemblance of God impressed upon the soul of man at his creation; that conformity to the divine character which is the proper end of redemption.

TSELEM — (Hebrew noun, H6754.) Image, likeness, representation. The keyword of Gen 1:26-27 (man created in the image of God); subsequently grounding the sanctity of human life (Gen 9:6), the equality of all bearers of the image, and the redemptive trajectory toward conformity to Christ, the perfect eikōn (Col 1:15).

And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness... So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.
Genesis 9:6

corruption_summary: The image-of-God doctrine is corrupted, in the contemporary moral landscape, by the systematic denial of the image in classes of human beings (the unborn killed in abortion, the disabled discarded as inconvenient, the elderly euthanized as no-longer-productive)—and by the ideological inflation of the image into a basis for autonomous self-definition that severs the image from its Creator and treats the bearer as the author of his own being.
corruption_paragraphs: The systematic denial of the image in classes of human beings is the most pressing contemporary corruption. The unborn child in the womb is, by biblical doctrine, an image-bearer from conception, and the deliberate killing of image-bearers (which abortion is) is the unjust shedding of innocent blood. The developmentally disabled person who cannot speak for himself is, by biblical doctrine, an image-bearer of equal dignity to the philosopher and the surgeon; the discarding of such persons as inconvenient or unproductive is the denial of the image. The elderly person whose productive capacities have declined is, by biblical doctrine, an image-bearer whose dignity is not measured by his output; the euthanizing of the elderly is the active denial of the image. The recovery of the image-doctrine is therefore one of the most pressing pastoral and political tasks of the present age: the unqualified affirmation that every human being, at every stage of life and in every condition, bears the image of God and is to be treated accordingly. The biblical sanctity of human life flows from this image-doctrine; remove the image, and the sanctity collapses; restore the image, and the sanctity is restored along with it.

The opposite contemporary corruption is the ideological inflation of the image into a basis for autonomous self-definition that severs the image from its Creator. Made in the image of God is read as: I have the inherent right to define myself however I choose, with my self-definition having the same dignity as God’s creation of me. The biblical doctrine refuses this. The image is given by the Creator; it is His image (not mine); it has a definite form (male and female, created and creaturely, designed and not self-authored); and the redemptive trajectory of the image is conformity to Christ, the perfect Image, not self-construction along whatever lines the bearer prefers. The contemporary identity-politics use of the image-language (the affirmation that every form of self-identification must be respected because each person is made in the image) is a corruption of the doctrine that has retained the vocabulary while reversing the substance. Recover both ends. Refuse the denial of the image in classes of human beings, and refuse the ideological inflation that severs the image from its Creator. The biblical image-doctrine is the foundation of human dignity precisely because it locates that dignity not in the bearer’s self-construction but in the Creator’s gift—a gift that grounds the sanctity of every human life and the trajectory of every redeemed soul toward conformity to the perfect Image Jesus Christ.
roots_summary: Hebrew tselem (image, likeness, representation), at Gen 1:26-27 the keyword of biblical anthropology; Greek eikōn the NT equivalent; tracing the structural arc from creation in the image, through the fall’s marring, to Christ the perfect image (Col 1:15) and the saints’ redemptive conformity to Him (Rom 8:29).

Hebrew d’mūth (H1823) — likeness, similitude (paired with tselem at Gen 1:26).
Greek eikōn (G1504) — image (Col 1:15; 3:10; 2 Cor 3:18; 4:4; Rom 8:29; 1 Cor 11:7; 15:49; Heb 1:3 cognate charaktēr).

usage: In the image of God created he him; male and female created he them—the foundational anthropological doctrine of every human bearing the image of God.
Christ is the perfect eikōn (Col 1:15), and the saints are being conformed to His image (Rom 8:29)—the image’s redemptive trajectory.

Denial of the image in classes of human beings (unborn, disabled, elderly) and ideological inflation severing the image from its Creator are opposite contemporary corruptions; biblical doctrine grounds dignity in the Creator’s gift, not in self-construction.
